title: Inheritance can narrow Italy’s generational wealth gap while preserving advantages of family origin
summary: Banca d’Italia researchers use Italian household surveys to show why the wealth held by older generations cannot be explained by ageing alone. Italians born in the 1940s and early 1950s accumulated more wealth over comparable stages of life than either earlier or later cohorts. Asset appreciation contributed substantially to the gains of the postwar generations, whereas younger households accumulated less and depended more heavily on saving from income. That difference matters because the generation that benefited from asset appreciation is now in a position to transfer it. The study estimates prospective transfers under stated assumptions. Its numbers describe potential family resources, rather than cash that younger households have already received and can deploy (Figures 2–6).

The authors construct age profiles from the 1991–2022 waves of the Survey on Household Income and Wealth. They compare generations at similar ages and separate age and birth-cohort patterns using an age–period–cohort model. They then allocate changes in household wealth between saving and capital gains, applying asset-specific returns to estimated holdings. Market conditions, including housing revaluations, can make two households with similar saving behaviour accumulate very different amounts. The calculation uses average returns for portfolios, so it cannot recover the price or timing of a particular household’s purchases. Identifying distinct age, period and cohort effects also requires restrictions because those three quantities are linked by construction (Sections 2–3, Appendix B).

The inheritance exercise pairs generations at representative ages. It asks what descendants aged 50–55 might receive if the corresponding parent generation passed on its resources at ages 75–80. Across successive child cohorts, potential inheritances as a share of the sum of own wealth and inheritance rose from 35% for those born in 1951–55 to 47% for those born in 1966–75. Family sizes, partnership patterns and the stock of parental wealth all matter. This ratio is neither the inheritance share of all Italian wealth nor a prediction about the timing of individual estates. Longer life, care spending and the timing of births can change the amount available or when a beneficiary receives it (Section 4, Table 1).

The distributional result depends on which households are compared. Education is used as a measure of family background, with generation-specific thresholds: at least lower-secondary education for parents and upper-secondary for recipients. In the youngest pairing, the ratio of average wealth for educated descendants of educated parents to that for less-educated descendants of less-educated parents falls from 3.5 to 2.5 after adding potential transfers. For descendants who both meet the higher education threshold, the ratio comparing those from educated and less-educated families instead rises from 1.5 to 1.6. An inheritance can represent a large fraction of a poorer family’s wealth while still transmitting an advantage between recipients with similar education (Table 2).

Holding parental wealth fixed and substituting the demographic structure of the earliest cohort changes the aggregate inheritance share very little for the youngest pairing. The offsetting group effects matter. The study’s decomposition of fertility and partnership changes suggests they reinforced advantages associated with better-educated family origins. The result offers a reason for lenders and wealth managers to distinguish housing equity and prospective assets from income and liquid assets available today. Nothing in the simulations establishes when households will sell inherited property, buy financial assets or alter their borrowing (Figure 8, Tables 1–4).

questions.question: When does prospective family wealth become spendable or usable as collateral?
questions.detail: The simulations assign transfers at representative ages and do not model the effect of longer lives or care spending. Link household survey histories with estate records, property transfers, gifts and age at receipt to estimate timing and liquidity. A prospective bequest decades away offers much less near-term support for a mortgage or investment account than a documented gift for a down payment.

questions.question: How dependent are the findings on the valuation of housing and other assets?
questions.detail: Capital gains contributed disproportionately to the postwar cohorts’ advantage, but sectoral returns are applied to surveyed portfolios. Compare property-register values, local transaction prices and household tenure histories, and test weaker house-price paths for the relevant regions. This would show how sensitive expected household balance sheets and intergenerational differences are to an asset-price correction.

questions.question: Does parental background predict transfers among households with similar education after conditioning on family structure?
questions.detail: The contrasting ratios hinge on who is compared, and a stylised allocation may conceal uneven transfers within families. Examine estate distributions, number of heirs, partnerships and education jointly using linked administrative or survey sources. Distinguishing unequal allocations from differences in the size of estates would clarify whether education narrows disparities in investable wealth as well as in earnings.
